scenes.name: Sugar Hill Records y Rapper’s Delight
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Sylvia Robinson, la «madre del hip hop», venía del R&B: Little Sylvia, el dúo Mickey & Sylvia («Love Is Strange», 1956), la producción del «It’s Gonna Work Out Fine» de Ike & Tina, el sello All Platinum con su marido Joe (con supuestos lazos mafiosos) y su propio éxito «Pillow Talk» (1973). Arruinada, vio a Lovebug Starski en Harlem World en 1979 y quiso grabar aquello; con Morris Levy fundaron Sugar Hill. Su hijo la llevó a una pizzería de Nueva Jersey donde Big Bank Hank, mánager de los Cold Crush, hizo una audición en su coche junto a Master Gee y Wonder Mike: la Sugarhill Gang. Sobre una recreación de «Good Times» de Chic grabaron quince minutos de rimas que una radio de St. Louis, WESL, se atrevió a poner: «Rapper’s Delight» inundó el mundo en otoño de 1979, dejó en anécdota el «King Tim III» de Fatback y demostró que el hip hop era negocio. En el Bronx sonaba a imitación higienizada: Hank rapeaba las rimas de Grandmaster Caz («I’m the C-A-S-AN, the O-V-A»), un estribillo de Hollywood y una frase de Rahiem; «hizo retroceder el hip hop cinco años» (Charlie Chase). Para Kool Moe Dee, sin Sugar Hill quizá no habría industria. La casa no pagaba bien a sus artistas, y su banda (Skip Alexander, Doug Wimbish, Duke Bootee) tocaba los temas. En Harlem, Bobby Robinson y su sello Enjoy ficharon a Flash, los Funky 4 + 1 y los Treacherous Three.

podcast.title: Acquisition of George Goldner's Companies
podcast.body: Levy initially owned 50% of George Goldner's record companies. As Goldner accumulated significant gambling debts, he used his record labels to pay them off, leading Levy to eventually acquire full ownership of all Goldner's companies, including any associated song rights. "Levy owned 50% of Goldeners record companies, and would soon vote at own all of them, as Goldener accumulated more gambling debts, and used his record labels to pay them off."

podcast.title: Attempt to Trademark "Rock and Roll"
podcast.body: Driven by his desire to monetize intellectual property, Levy collaborated with his friend Alan Freed in an attempt to trademark the phrase "rock and roll." Their aim was to force any record labeled as such to pay them for its usage, but the term spread too rapidly to be successfully enforced. "Indeed, Levy was so keen to make money after UBS intellectual property, that he actually formed a company with his friend Alan Fried, which attempted to trademark the phrase rock and roll."

podcast.title: Founding Birdland and Music Publishing
podcast.body: In the 1940s, Levy founded Birdland, the world-famous jazz club. When ASCAP sought performance royalties for songwriters, Levy immediately recognized the profit potential in music publishing. He subsequently established his own publishing company, Patricia Music, and record label, Roulette, specifically to exploit artists' intellectual property for long-term gain. "Levy had been the founder of Birdland, the world famous jazz club, in the 1940s, but when ASCAP came to him... Levy had immediately seen the possibilities in music publishing."

podcast.title: Mafia Connections and Artist Exploitation
podcast.body: Morris Levy is described as one of the worst figures in music history, a terrible human being and a con artist who leveraged his mafia connections to ensure that artists he exploited would never dare to sue him, valuing their lives over legal recourse. This made him a particularly dangerous force for young, unprivileged artists. "Maris Levy was a terrible human being and a con artist, so someone who used his mafia connections to ensure that the artist's seripped off would never even think of suing him, because they valued their lives too much."

podcast.title: Role in Song Promotion
podcast.body: Levy's close friend, Alan Freed, played a crucial role in the success of The Teenagers' "Why Do Fools Fall in Love" by providing a substantial promotional push for the record. "helped by a massive push from Marvis Levy's good friend Alan Fried."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 35: "Why Do Fools Fall In Love?" by Frankie Lymon and the Teenagers

podcast.title: Threats and Control Over Artists
podcast.body: Levy's methods involved extreme intimidation; there are multiple reports of artists receiving death threats, being forced to abandon their careers, or moving thousands of miles away to escape his revenge if they defied him. This control made him a formidable figure, especially against vulnerable, teenage Black artists. "There are several people who report death threat, or having to give up their careers, or suddenly move thousands of miles away from home, to avoid Levy's revenge on artists who didn't do exactly what he said."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Uncredited Co-writer for "Why Do Fools Fall in Love"
podcast.body: Levy became the legal co-writer of "Why Do Fools Fall in Love" by acquiring George Goldner's credited rights to the song, despite never having heard it until it had already become a massive hit. He thus profited significantly from a song he had no part in creating. "But when Levy bought out Goldner's holdings in his companies, he also bought out his rights to songs he was credited for, so Levy became the legal co-writer of Why the Fools Fall in Love."
